utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out in English a short summary of the -- of this witness's statement. [In English] Witness KW586 was a member of a unit of the Bosnian army called Biseri. The task of the unit was to protect the Presidency, its members, and their families. During his shifts, KW586 was constantly with President Izetbegovic and he was present during many of the secret meetings held in the basement of the National Bank. These meetings were attended by military and political leaders as well as by Izetbegovic's son, Bakir; Izetbegovic's son-in-law, Jasmin; and Reis-ul-ulema Ceric, who had the biggest influence on the president because he was a believer and he held the Reis-ul-ulema in deep respect. From the first meeting he attended as a security guard, KW586 heard that the goal of President Izetbegovic and the other leaders was to get the international community militarily involved in BH on the Bosnian side. To achieve this goal, they decided to apply the tactic of causing the mass suffering of the Bosnian population and of engaging in provocations in order to cause the shelling of buildings such as hospitals and the like. They agreed to provoke the Serbs who had a lot of artillery on positions around Sarajevo, so they would engage in shelling which in turn would be used against them before the international community. Whenever shelling was provoked in the places where civilians would be hurt, the TV crews and journalists would be close by. Furthermore, smaller units were to make incursions into Serbian-populated areas, where they would attack the civilian population in order to get a reaction from the Serbian forces. This strategy involved the engagement of units of the local commanders with a criminal past such as Juka Prazina, Caco, Celo Bajramovic, and others. These men were supposed to do as much dirty work in Sarajevo against the Serbs as possible before the regular units with a joint command were formed so that their actions would be qualified as crime and revenge and President Izetbegovic could not be held responsible. The truce agreed between the Muslims and the Croats just before the Washington Agreement was a condition for a large quantity of weapons intended for the Muslims and located in Split on the Adriatic coast, to cross Herceg-Bosna on trucks and get to Sarajevo. In addition to the weapons transported from Croatia to Bosnia with trailer-trucks, weapons were also normally packed into food and clothing which was supplied as humanitarian aid. In the spring of 1994, President Izetbegovic and Reis-ul-ulema Ceric met Naser Oric in order to remind him of the importance of provoking the international intervention in BH. They suggested Oric to organise smaller combat groups which would leave the safe area without the knowledge of the UNPROFOR and engage in combat actions against civilians in Serbian-populated communities as to provoke the Serbian forces into retaliating and shelling the safe areas. The victims were not important. As Reis-ul-ulema Ceric often repeated: They are dying for a just cause and on the part of the Lord. Soon after KW586 heard this conversation, news started arriving that the Srebrenica had been shelled by the Serbian forces. In some of those cases there was even talk that Muslim forces had shelled parts of Srebrenica to point the finger at the Serbs. The implementation of the agreed tactic to constantly provoke the other side and have the international community blame the Serbs included the staging of incidents before or during the visits of international officials. As for the first Markale incident, Witness KW586 personally heard President Izetbegovic, Reis-ul-ulema Ceric, and others present in the bank talking what could have happened if a shell were to fall on Markale because the market was full of people. Two or three days after this meeting a shell impacted at the Markale market. And that is short summary. Now I would like to pose several questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us from when until when were you a member of this protection unit, unit for the protection of the Presidency and the members of the Presidency and their families?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Two years, from April or May 1992 until May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until when did President Izetbegovic use the shelter at the bank?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: As far as I know, the whole period I was there he was also at the bank. I didn't notice that he was moved during my tenure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have received a document from the Presidency -- sorry, from the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina which says he used the bank premises until June 1993. Which information is correct, what you have just told us or what is written in this letter?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not moved as long as I was there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1D8845. No broadcast until I say something can be broadcast.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: While we're waiting, can you tell us, Witness, after the war did you suffer any health problems; and if so, what kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any consequences; and if so, what kind?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: I have this tremor still in my hand and in one foot, but no other consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we don't have this in e-court, could this document be placed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We have it in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will now read out to you, it says, pertaining to your request for assistance - please do not broadcast this - I will read it out in English so it can be interpreted to you. [In English] The witness "is a qualified driver. During 20th of May, 1992 - 12th of May, 1994" this witness "was a member of the Protection of People and Objects ... of the Interior Ministry of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the basis of the decision made by the Interior Ministry of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of," with this date, witness "was a reserve policeman of the Protection of People and Objects Sector - Police Unit for the Protection of People and Objects and he was a sergeant beginning with 1st September, 1993 ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "... a member of the Fifth Police Department in the Interior Ministry of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina beginning with the 12th of May, 1994. "Finally" this witness "was a member of the unit 'Biseri' throughout the war in B and H, and the unit was responsible for the protection of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina." [Interpretation] Is this information consistent with what you know? Is it true, in other words?

utterances.speaker: KW586

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: KW586

What I'm trying to say is that the unit Biseri existed 20 days before this, but this is the official date of its inception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we met on Saturday; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I want to ask you about some of the things that you told us on Saturday and maybe get you to confirm some of that information, but maybe I can get you to close that thing that's on the desk in front of you so you're not going to be distracted. All right? Great. Thank you. Now, first of all, since you had this stroke that you told Dr. Karadzic about, you've had a little bit of trouble with your memory, right, because you told us on Saturday you have problems with dates?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: No, no. Not that. Generally speaking, during the war we weren't sure what the date was at which particular time. We weren't watching the news on TV and we weren't able to keep track of the dates in that sense. It has nothing to do with my health. Even when I was there in that period of time, I didn't know what the date was. The only thing of paramount importance was to survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To survive what?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: The shelling, sniping. You know yourself, everything that the war brings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now just to go back to my question. It's true, isn't it then, what you told us on Saturday. On Saturday you said: I don't remember any date. If someone were to ask me dates, I don't remember. That's true; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: But only the dates during the war, not after. This is not a consequence of my stroke. I had my stroke in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you work after your stroke?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Do you mean in the company I was working for?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you -- after you had a stroke you were off work for a while; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: however, I didn't continue working after my stroke. I was retired.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have lines 7 and 8 redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, just in case, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you haven't had a job since at least 2001; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Right. I have never worked again after 2001. I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. And you've been watching this trial, haven't you? You told us that on Saturday. You've been watching it on the internet and you've been watching it on TV; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: That's not right. I only said that through BN TV one can follow the trial regularly. I didn't say that I myself followed it. What I meant to say was that the people over there are fully familiar with everything that is happening here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, when we asked you how you got in contact with Dr. Karadzic's Defence team, you said that you knew who they were because you spent a lot of time watching the trial, that the trial was being broadcast constantly on BN TV. And so that's how you recognised who the Defence counsel of Dr. Karadzic were. That's actually what you told us on Saturday; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I said that I watched it occasionally, I mean the trial. Besides, all of us know who the counsel are and we know about the accused. There are TV shows discussing what somebody's guilty of or not, so it's a thing that one necessarily has to know. It's not that I was following the trial regularly; it was occasionally that I would watch what was happening. There was no need for me to follow it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's how you knew who the counsel were and that's how you went and contacted Mr. Petronijevic, who's here in court; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petronijevic is always featured on one of these TV channels.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So he didn't find you to testify; you went to find him. Right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You explained to us now on Saturday that when you went to Germany after leaving Sarajevo, you stayed there for only around a month; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: A month or two, I don't know. I don't know if it makes any difference, but that's correct. I wasn't able to obtain any rights so I moved to Belgium.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you -- in Germany you never claimed asylum as a refugee?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, no, but it was all in the hands of my sister. She took charge of it all. She was trying to obtain papers for me to stay there. I don't know what she resorted to, but she was going through all the ways and means of keeping me in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're not able to confirm whether or not you claimed asylum as a refugee; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know what she applied for, whether it was for asylum or merely for a permit of residence. I know that she went to several municipalities filing applications in order to keep me there. They were very reluctant to accept refugees at the time. The war was nearing its end and they were already thinking of sending the refugees they already had back.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, this is -- you know, if what you say is true, this is a pretty important story about a conspiracy that could have affected -- if it broke could have affected the conduct of parts of the rest of the war. And it could have affected your stay in Germany, and you never told this story to the authorities in Germany, did you?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: I never discussed the war with anyone in Germany, not with the authorities, not with the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, the story you're giving us today is kind of like the ultimate conspiracy about the war involving everybody from the political leadership to the military leadership to the media. If what you say is true, that story could have stopped more people from dying in Sarajevo, it could have stopped more people from dying in Srebrenica, and you didn't think it was important enough to tell as soon as you landed in Germany?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Well, no. It's always this question of to be or not to be. At first I did not consider that I should say anything at all because it was the same on both sides, and they were doing what they were doing while we were doing what we were doing. And I thought there was a balance to it all. But when I saw after the war that the same gang is ruling Sarajevo just as it did during the war, although the war had ended, while other people are being held accountable for what they had done, then I saw there was no balance in it after all. If one who is liable is held to account, then another one should be held to account as well. And when I saw that injustice, then I changed my mind. And even then, it's very difficult to say things against your own people. I wouldn't wish it upon anyone, but sometimes you have to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If it could have saved lives of your own people, wouldn't it have been worth saying 20 years ago when you first landed in Europe?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: I just told you. Whether it is right or not, I don't know, but at that time I was still not certain that I should do it. I wasn't even thinking of doing it. I wasn't even thinking of whether I should. It was all fresh in my head and my only thought was to get away from it, to find shelter with my family, to get as far away as I could from the war. I didn't think about it at all. And at that time the Hague Tribunal still did not exist anyway, so it didn't occur to me to do anything further with that story. I just didn't think about it. I simply wanted to find some peace of mind, to get some rest from all of that, to find my own spiritual peace and then to get better physically, to recover my weight. I wasn't thinking really, if you can understand, whether what was right and what was not, not during those years. And only later when I saw that some people are being judged for crimes that they hadn't done while others were not being judged for crimes they were responsible for, then -- then it came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, a month or two after you got to Germany, you left for Belgium; that's what you told us Saturday, right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you lived there for five years, four and a half or five years, not even 200 kilometres away from this Tribunal, and you never told the Belgian authorities this great conspiracy story, did you?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: No, no, no. But I'm telling you now. At that moment -- well, I've already told you, I was just looking at my own personal interest, to get some rest, to come to. You can condemn me all you want, but it never really crossed my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: But, but, there is this other reason, what I said just now, let everybody be responsible. That's my opinion. Nobody was accused then. These judgements came later. Everybody should be responsible for everything; Mr. Karadzic too. If he's guilty for anything, let him be held accountable, but don't make him guilty for the things he didn't do. That's it. As for these years, I never thought of testifying, saying things. And then when these judgements were being passed, then I sort of thought about it. I saw that over all of those 20 years that gang is still in power over there, no one can touch them. So that led to it too, but that came only later --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: -- it wasn't at first.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, so if what you're saying is true, you weren't thinking clearly - because that's what you said - for the whole five years you were in Belgium --

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. No, it's not that I wasn't thinking. I wasn't thinking about war, The Hague. I just wanted to distance myself from all of that, to be as far away from it as I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And sacrifice the people that you left behind when you fled Sarajevo; that's what you did, right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Well, I guess you have to say that. I couldn't have changed anything, just like anybody else. But anyway, if that's what you're saying then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So two months after you left Germany there were people on the ground here in The Hague at this Tribunal. The whole time you were living in Belgium, we were operating. And you would have seen that Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic, while you were living in Belgium, were indicted for killing and terrorising civilians in Sarajevo, by shelling and sniping, and for the killings in Srebrenica, and you just stayed there; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Yes, just stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You didn't think this story was important enough to get on the train for an hour and a half and come speak to an investigator here, did you?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: First of all, I'm saying now I did not follow the news very much, either this way or that way. So it wasn't that I was informed about The Hague -- well, even if I had been informed, during that first time I wasn't really interested in that until these wrong judgements started coming in. Well, then, I saw that one was being held accountable but not the other one, and in my view both should be held accountable but I saw that only later when I came to Bosnia that none of those bandits of ours are being held accountable and others are. Well, call it what you will. While I was in Belgium, it never crossed my mind that I should go and say something to someone. I just tried to forget all of that. It was only when I returned to Sarajevo and when I saw that those same people that were looting, that had a free hand then, it is only then that I felt this revolt again. Now, whatever you say to that, however you may interpret this, that's the way it was. But in Belgium, it never crossed by mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, when you went back to Sarajevo, as you told us on Saturday, in 1999, these people who you mention in your statement - I'll give you two examples - Sefer Halilovic, he was put on trial in this Tribunal in 2005 and you didn't come forward. Naser Oric, who you talk about a lot in your statement, was put on trial in 2006 and you had a story that could have changed the course of his trial and you didn't come forward. That's because, Mr. Witness, you were only thinking about yourself, just like you're only thinking about yourself in coming forward now after 20 years. That's really what's going on, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, then you --

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: I don't know how come. Thank you. That's not the way it is. In order to understand all of that, you have to live in Bosnia for a while. Roughly around 2000 I wanted to come here for the first time, and I said that to some people, that I intended to make a statement against that scum over there. And then, as we talked, quite a lot of people agreed with that but very few would come and dare testify. The main reason is that they all have their families there, they have children, and nobody dares because they know that there would be a lot of retaliation. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm not asking about other people; I'm asking about you. You didn't come forward -- Mr. Witness, you have protective measures. Please, let's try and not talk over one another. You didn't come forward to testify in the trial of Naser Oric because you're making this up.

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: No way, no. You can interpret that any which way you want, whether I'm right or wrong, but what I said is the truth. And if you allow me, I will continue saying what I tried to say a moment ago. I wanted to come here roughly in 2000, and as I talked to all these other people who were not interested, they all agreed that there's been an injustice but nobody dares testify. I hope that after my testimony perhaps one or two more people will come and there will be some purpose in all of this, otherwise nobody can get rid of that gang over there. I did want to come in 2000 and I confided (redacted) (redacted) I said that I would testify. He said that to them. The very next day, the very next day around the apartment there were jeeps, there were threats: What are you doing, you ape? What are you doing, playing with your life? Where do you think you're going, you fool? Things like that. And this was going round and round.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name in lines 9 and 10, could that be redacted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you can't even get your story straight between Saturday and today. On Saturday you told my colleague who was interviewing you exactly this same story, but you said it happened in 2012 and not in 2000.

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Obviously you misunderstood all of that. I know exactly what it was that I said, and I spoke about the first time, about that which is now. As for the rest, the story that coincides with 2012, I know exactly what I said. I wanted in 2001 to testify, but they prevented me from doing so. And then came that stroke, and that's why I couldn't afterwards. But once I recovered from this stoke and when I saw that I could -- and you see that it's a bit hard for me to walk even now. Again I spoke up. And that's why this testimony of mine did not arrive on time for Oric and Halilovic, that's the only reason. I know full well what it was that I said because that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On Saturday we didn't ask you about 2000 or 2001; we were asking you about Halilovic and Oric in 2006. And you said on Saturday that you told this great story only in 2012 to your one cousin, so you told one person, and you thought that he must have told someone because immediately afterwards jeeps showed up. And then I asked you, I asked you, who he told, and you had absolutely no idea. You can't tell me who he told, you can't told me where he spoke to them, you can't tell me even if he told someone because it never happened, Mr. Witness; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: That's not right. You've twisted it. Perhaps I misunderstood you there, but I know what I'm saying now and that is the way it is. It did happen. That is contained in my statement, and you did not allow me to say a bit more. When I wanted to tell you more on Saturday, you just said: Okay, okay, let's move on and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then tell us who your cousin told.

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Who he told? How could I know? I just know that this gang is very well organised and that very quickly they got these yes men of theirs, probably somebody who's in cahoots with the people that I'm testifying about. Only a day before that there weren't any jeeps and the very next day there were jeeps and threats, and I hadn't told anyone but him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Witness, since the 1990s this Tribunal has had an office in Sarajevo open to the public in a protected facility. The people in our office in Sarajevo include staff who have specific witness protection skills and training, and you never in all the 13 years you were living in Bosnia showed up with this huge conspiracy story; right? You never went to them?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: I never did, never did. Should I comment upon that or ... ?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to go to another thing -- another area that we talked about on Saturday. You confirmed on Saturday, didn't you, that you were not one of President Izetbegovic's body-guards; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Well, this word, "body-guard," that would be wrong. I was just a guard, an escort -- well, "body-guard," wow.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the president, he had a lot of meetings, didn't he, meetings that you wouldn't have known about; right ?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's because you weren't with him all the time; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you know that if he was really concerned about information leaking out about something sensitive, he would have closed-door meetings that nobody could overhear. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, well --

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: That room --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- Mr. Witness, you know that because you talked about a meeting like that in your statement. That's what the president did. If he didn't want -- if he was discussing highly sensitive information, he would have closed-door meetings, just like the one you talked about that he had with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Tudjman never came to that room in the bank. Tudjman was at the Presidency, and that's completely different. You're confusing things. In this room where Izetbegovic lived, in the basement of the bank, there were these persons who were mentioned here that came, starting with the Reis and Bakir and Sefer Talijan. The meeting with Tudjman was an official visit. However, they within the Presidency had their meeting somewhere up there at the Presidency. This has nothing to do with this thing over here. There's nothing for me to say there. Whereas over here in the basement of the bank, well that is where they decided what they decided. Whether they hid that from me, no. I guess they trusted me or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's get --

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: But I could hear every word. Tudjman has nothing to do with this whole story. He was just mentioned because of the weapons. Later when that meeting was held with him -- well, seven days later, those weapons were released from Split -- well, that's the only context for Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll leave that conspiracy aside and get back to my question. You would agree, would you, that the president would have closed-door meetings where he didn't want to have anybody overhear; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you wouldn't describe yourself as a close confidant of Sefer Halilovic, would you? You weren't Sefer Halilovic's closest friend or in his inner circle, were you?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The same with Ismet Dahic, you weren't a close confidant of Ismet Dahic?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the same goes, doesn't it, for Avdo Hebib, Stjepan Kljuic, Mustafa Hajrulahovic, even Reis-ul-ulema Ceric, Bakir, Izetbegovic? You are not a close confidant of any of those people and you weren't at the time, were you?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Well, I was nothing with them. I hadn't known these people from before. Quite simply, I was carrying out my duties and it so happened that in the course of my work I would be close to the president. As for this man, I can only say the best and even later, and you can see that from my statement. I think even -- since he's a religious man, had somebody asked him -- I think he would have repeated that here too, but there you go. I was no friend of theirs. I hadn't known anyone from before. I mean, we weren't friends or enemies. Quite simply, I was on this guard duty 3 or 4 metres away from them, and as far as I know the late President Alija was always very nice to me. He'd bring me a cup of tea and sometimes we'd even exchange a word or two, in a friendly way really. (redacted) so probably that's why I had that duty too. It wasn't for Sefer or anybody else, it was just Ari Slupovac [phoen] as commander of the president's guard and the Presidency. He's the only one who would decide who would go where. No one could interfere with that, Sefer or this person or that person.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that an explicit instruction to Naser Oric to attack Serb civilians to provoke the Serbs into shelling a safe area and Sefer Halilovic openly saying that he had fired a shell at the market-place and was going to do so again would be incredibly damaging to the interests of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, wouldn't it? If that came out, that would be incredibly damaging. It would turn world opinion against them, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: That requires a broader explanation. Will you allow me? Alija Izetbegovic was convinced that he could not win this war because he had a lot of men but less weapons. And the point was always to somehow provoke an international intervention in this or that way, according to the motto: All's fair in war. That's what was aimed at, to cause an international intervention even at the cost of one's own victims. The first time we expected international intervention, President Mitterrand of France came and nothing happened. There was no intervention. Then after that there would be a few casualties here, a few casualties there, but it was never even remotely enough for the international community to intervene. Now, on the basis of all of that, because these two towns were -- well, Srebrenica was a protected area and Gorazde was a protected area, and then there's Sarajevo. They were the ones that the media wrote about the most, abroad as well. And also according to that thing, everything goes in war, just win the battle, I know when the Reis said that, well I saw that. Daily we're losing 50 to 70 people and no use, whereas this way if we managed to provoke an international intervention they will all go to paradise, they will all be martyrs on God's path. Those are his words. So that was the point of all of that, to provoke an international intervention and that could be done only through the protected areas. In Gorazde they didn't succeed in that because they didn't have a man they trusted there who would obey them the way Oric did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question --

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. My question was: If this news, if your story had leaked out, that would have been incredibly damaging and turned world opinion against the Bosnian people, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Probably. If that is just -- if -- well, if it's possible to answer just that way -- well, yes, yes, that would be right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So -- but your evidence -- and it would be pretty basic to have these conversations actually behind closed doors, just like the president did with President Tudjman; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Again, I'm saying Tudjman is a completely different story and the president had a meeting, a real meeting, with Tudjman in a real building, the building of the Presidency of BH, where these decisions were made; whereas these other meetings were held in the basement of the bank - do you understand that? - where Alija lived temporarily because over there his apartment had been shelled. And those decisions that were made at the Presidency had nothing to do with these decisions taken at the bank. It's just that some chosen people came to the bank. When Oric came, he never stopped at the Presidency building, never. I remember three times when he was there and once I brought him by car from Dobrinja to the runway, to the Holiday Inn, and over there he never went to the Presidency building but he always came to meetings at the bank. I want to tell you to make a distinction between the two, and over here, it was only these six or seven men who came to the bank, at first Kljuic. After that he didn't come, when he realised what was going on there he said: I don't want anything to do with that, whereas those people came non-stop. Do you understand that? Where can you have a greater conspiracy than the bank basement? There was no journalists there, secretaries, no one, just six or seven men talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: And I.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your evidence -- and your evidence is that they discussed these plans that could turn world opinion against them over and over and over again in front of you; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: If that's what you say, that's the way it is. I don't know what could turn out, but there you go.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you're the first one to come forward with this story that they discussed, not behind closed doors, you're the first one to come forward with this story in 20 years; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: I don't know whether I'm the first one or which one I am. I just know that that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note it's actually past the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue after a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just add one more thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll continue after the break. We'll resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I want to talk about some of these shelling provocations you described in your statement, your written evidence. And you said, with respect to those incidents: "The agreement was that whenever shelling like this was provoked in the places where civilians would be hurt, TV crews and journalists would be close by." So as I understand that, it's your position that these incidents were all pre-planned in arrangements with TV journalists; that's your evidence, right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: No. The journalists didn't know anything about it. Our people just made sure that they would be close by when an incident would happen so they could report in time, and since Sarajevo was encircled it was never far away from the Presidency to the Dvor, to Kosevo, to all these addresses, and the journalists were always at the ready to go there. Of course the journalists had nothing to do with it. They just wrote about what they saw, and our people served them up what they should see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, do you mean you? You've just said: "Our people made sure they would be close by when an incident would happen ..." How would you know if you weren't a part of it?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: I could neither decide anything nor was I able to -- I was just close by when somebody discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, then how do you know that your people made sure that journalists would be close by when an incident would happen? Tell me what they did to make sure that happened?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know what they did later because I wasn't there after. I only know when they talked amongst themselves how to take care of the journalists, and generally speaking, Avdo Hebib took care of journalists while he was there. That was his assignment, to enable all the journalists to go whenever they wanted to, that access not be denied to them. But, first of all, our people were supposed to clean things up so the journalists shouldn't see what they shouldn't see, the military hospital and all the other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh. But --

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: -- the buildings of all the institutions, but not for a moment did I say that journalists were pre-advised or involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this arrangement, this agreement that you're talking about, if it's true, that would involve, I would say probably at a minimum, some senior police officials, some senior military officials, probably some brigade officials, probably some traffic cops from different parts of the city of Sarajevo, probably the crew who was driving the truck that the weapon was launched on and the crew that fired it, and you're the first one from inside Sarajevo to come out and talk about this; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: All these who were enumerated probably should have known, but all these people were just executing orders without asking why. You understand? I don't know about what came after. I only know what I saw and heard at these meetings. What happened later at the execution stage I was not able to know because I wasn't there. I could only know when they said: Oh, this job was well done or that job was well done. And I know who was in charge of what. A moment ago you said Sefer Halilovic fired that shell; Sefer Halilovic didn't, the Italian did, Mustafa Hajrulahovic, on the orders of Sefer Halilovic and those others in the basement. That's the small error you made.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, so now when you talk about Markale I, you've pulled General Hajrulahovic into the story. Were you there? Because that's the only reason you would know about any order that General Hajrulahovic might have given. Did you see him give the order?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: When we were in the building of the Presidency and when the planning was done for that, then Alija told Sefer: This and that needs to be done. Sefer turned towards the Italian and said: No problem, the Italian will take care of it. That's the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: And similarly, when the first attempt was made - there were two attempts - the first attempt with that shell ended in the shell landing on a roof near the market. The same thing was said: No problem, we'll repeat it. We just have to wait for the same conditions to meet, for the same group of UNPROFOR to be near. That's how I know it was the Italian, not Sefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So let's leave the media conspiracy and let's go on and talk about the Markale conspiracy.

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. No, there was no media conspiracy, no media conspiracy at all. The media just covered and broadcast what we served them, and I include myself in that army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's talk about Markale I. You're saying that the shell that fell on the market-place in Sarajevo in February 1994 was fired - because this is how I read your evidence - it was fired from Bosnian army positions under Mrkovici by Mustafa Hajrulahovic at the order of Sefer Halilovic and with the knowledge of an entire UNPROFOR team; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: No, no. No, I did not mention the UNPROFOR in that context. That UNPROFOR team was chosen perhaps because they were less attentive in listening for the shells or because they were drunk. I don't know why they were chosen by our people. But after that one visit of the UNPROFOR our people knew who and what they were. There was no UNPROFOR conspiracy. I don't know why they needed that particular team, by that, that crew of people who were counting the shells. For the rest, you are correct, everything apart from the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you said in your statement why they needed that UNPROFOR team. You said that they had some kind of agreements with them that they wouldn't register the firing of missiles from our positions, so UNPROFOR was part of the conspiracy you're alleging in your own words?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: I never said that, and if it's written somewhere then it needs to be corrected. I never said that the UNPROFOR was part of the conspiracy; UNPROFOR wasn't. It's just that one crew, I don't know whether they were a bit careless or less attentive, but nobody ever said that UNPROFOR was part of the conspiracy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have the witness's statement in his own language so he could have a look at that sentence that he seems to be having trouble with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course, by all means, but shall we upload it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's at paragraph 8, B/C/S page 10.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not to broadcast. Not to broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Last page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in your language, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 10 --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think it's about seven lines up from the bottom. And it says, and I quote: "They had some kind of agreements with them," referring to UNPROFOR," that they would not register the firing of missiles from our positions."

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Yes, but the crew of the UNPROFOR, not the whole UNPROFOR. And these two or three men could be drunk, they could be inattentive, they could be whatever, not the whole UNPROFOR but just one team. The way you put it, it sounds like the whole UNPROFOR conspired against the Serbs. It was just one crew, two or three men. I don't know how many there are in one crew.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this third or fourth conspiracy that you're alleging would involve Halilovic, Hajrulahovic, at least one subordinate officer, a mortar crew, police who would make sure that no one who was living in the area saw what was going on, or civilians in Sedrenik who were living just hundreds of metres from where you say this shell should have been fired, and the UNPROFOR team; right? That's who would have been involved in this scenario that you're putting to us today.

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Mrkovici village was chosen because it was known from before that there were mortar positions there, and it was important to occupy a couple of positions covering certain axes. And since the separation lines were very close, it's very difficult to decide whether a missile targeted a place here or 2- or 300 metres away. And for the inhabitants of Sedrenik --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This scenario potentially involves the conspiracy of dozens of people from all walks of life, right, the scenario that you're putting to us today; right?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Let me explain this scenario and then we'll see how we go on. You can't just ask me to say yes or no. Will you let me explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You explain what you want.

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: The direction of Mrkovici village was chosen because a number of times during the war shelling came from that side. The distance between separation lines was very small so it's very difficult to decide whether it was fired from Mrkovici or not in the direction of Markale. And I believe the inhabitants of Sedrenik didn't pay attention at all. What they cared about was that the shell didn't fall on them because there were shells non-stop falling, so they are certainly not part of the conspiracy. As for the rest, I can only tell you what they discussed at their meetings. I did not go out into the field and check any further. I know that it was agreed when they talked amongst themselves that Mrkovici village would be chosen. It would be good because there had been firing at the city from that village before and because they knew there were mortars there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: And whether those others down there were part of the conspiracy -- no, they didn't have to know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this account, just like most of your statement and every single conspiracy you allege, is pure fiction because you would know that at the time you said these discussions were going on, Sefer Halilovic wasn't even in the army. He had been ostracised months before. He had been dismissed from the army at the time this was going on. You made it up, just like every other conspiracy you've alleged to try and get yourself a better deal with the people who are protecting you now. That's what's going on, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: No, no, regardless of how you want to present it. I know that with time you will get that other information. And I'm sure you already know a lot that would make you believe what I'm saying. I said that Halilovic was ostracised because of certain things he did vis-a-vis the Croats and the honest officers insisted he be removed. Alija, under pressure, removed him but could not dismiss him from the army. Alija knew that he had to do because of the other members of the Presidency, and under the strong pressure of the officers who were not in on all of this, he removed him. He brought in Rasim Delic instead, a person who was not from Sarajevo, to be commander in Sarajevo. And Sefer continued to hold the rank he did before when he was the Commander-in-Chief. But they explained to him nicely that they had to replace him. And I didn't say that he was in Sarajevo all the time. But whenever he was in Sarajevo, he would come by. Sometimes he was outside Sarajevo, sometimes not. They didn't always attend all the meetings in full compositions. Kljuic came the first few times, but when he saw it was going on he said he would not be a part of it anymore. And I think if you called him, he would confirm what I'm saying. I know that this is the way it happened. Now it's up to you to prove.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, the issue just discussed about Sefer Halilovic, on what terms were Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Halilovic before and after he stepped down from his position as the Commander-in-Chief?

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: Well, it was the same, it didn't change. Alija appointed Halilovic as the Commander-in-Chief precisely because he could do with him whatever he wanted. Sefer, as one of the most junior officers, was the least-deserving of being appointed as the Commander-in-Chief. But Alija appointed him precisely for the fact that he could manipulate him as he wished. Halilovic was rubbish and he was very ambitious. And as -- he was really a scumbag, and there was stories that I heard about crimes being committed by our army. So under the pressure from Croats, Alija simply had to remove Sefer. So he was set aside but let alone to do exactly what he had been doing up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: KW586
utterances.text: May I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Mr. Witness. That concludes your evidence, sir. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. Shall we adjourn for how many minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 11.33 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, the Chamber would like now to address an issue stemming from the accused's motion to admit testimony of Borivoje Jakovljevic pursuant to Rule 92 quater filed on the 21st of January, 2014, and the Prosecution's response to the motion filed on the 3rd of February. In the motion, the accused submits that the witness is unavailable to testify before the Chamber due to the fact that he underwent brain surgery in July 2013 and no longer has a good memory about the events to which he testified in a prior case before the Tribunal. While the accused attaches to the motion a report from the witness's family doctor, noting the witness's unavailability to testify, the Chamber notes that such a report is based on other medical documentation also attached to the motion, and nowhere in such documentation has the Chamber been able to find a reference to a medical condition which would support for the witness's unavailability to testify. It is therefore the Chamber's position that it requires additional medical documentation before being able to rule on the motion. The Chamber notes the accused's suggestion in the motion that if the Chamber decided the need for the witness to undergo further medical examination, he should order it at the Chamber's own expense. However, it is not for the Chamber but for the relevant party, in this case the accused, to obtain all the supporting material for his requests. Let's bring in the next witness. The next witness is Mr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, it's Mr. Glamocic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic has been fixed tomorrow morning for 9.00, and we thought it was not good to have him waiting in detention here. So we may finish a little bit early today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll communicate with Mr. Robinson about the schedule. That's generally true. I was considering the possibility of a slight adjustment. I'll communicate with him by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I forgot to mention and put on the record that the Chamber conveyed the -- its order to redact certain parts of the previous witness's statement via e-mail. I just wanted to confirm it, but I forgot that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And also, Mr. President, the upcoming witness's testimony you have ordered the redaction of paragraphs 3 through 11, which we've done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Glamocic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. I take it that you understand my words in your language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Glamocic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us please wait for the interpretation to finish and you will be able to observe that on your screen. Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 1D08850.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the first page of your statement that you see on the screen? Do not be confused by the fact that some of the paragraphs have been struck off. It's because the Chamber did not feel that they were relevant. Is this the first page of your statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the last page be shown so that the witness may identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully convey your words. For your information, the paragraphs 3 up to and including paragraph 11 have been excluded from your statement. Does this statement faithfully reflect your words?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you about the same things and put the same questions to you, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender the statement into evidence under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4379, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out in English a short summary of the statement of Mr. Vladimir Glamocic. [In English] Vladimir Glamocic was elected chairman of the Executive Committee of the Knezevo Municipal Assembly, Skender Vakuf known as early -- in 1991. He held this position until 1993 when he went to work at the directorate of roads of the Republika Srpska. In 1990, Serbs made up about 70 per cent of the population of Knezevo municipality --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Pardon the interruption --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I believe that Dr. Karadzic would save time as well by skipping the second and third paragraphs of the 65 ter summary which were excluded from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I kept the old one. [In English] From the beginning of the conflict in Slovenia and later in Croatia and BH, civilian and military convoys were often travelled through the territory of Knezevo municipality. No one ever notified the local government when the convoys would pass and where the people in it were from. From the beginning of this term the -- of office of the chairman of the Executive Committee of the Knezevo municipality, Mr. Glamocic tried to establish good relations with the neighbouring municipalities of Travnik and Jajce mainly inhabited by Muslims and Croats and succeeded in it to a significant degree. The municipal authorities in these municipalities were headed by the elected representatives of Croats and Muslim population. The municipal leaders of Knezevo enjoyed the full support of President Karadzic in terms of maintaining good relations with the neighbouring municipalities. President Karadzic phoned Mr. Glamocic in the early hours of 23rd of August, 1992, after being informed of the incident that occurred at the Koricanske Stijene on the 21st of August. On the same day Mr. Glamocic went out to the scene with the chief of the civilian protection and the VRS in order to investigate the situation and take measures. Since during the war members of the civilian protection were mostly older men unfit for military service, the municipality did not have either the human or financial resources to deal with the problem of pulling out the dead bodies and burying them. That is why the president of the municipality Assembly got in contact with the authorities of the ARK in order to find a solution at the regional level, while Mr. Glamocic was responsible for mobilising the forces of the municipality. Mr. Glamocic participated in a meeting held at the Banja Luka Security Service Centre, CSB, and chaired by Minister of Defence, General Subotic. The meeting was dedicated to the solving of the problem at Koricanske Stijene because Knezevo municipality was unable to solve it alone. During the meeting, the president of Prijedor municipality, Mr. Stakic, pointed out that the conflict created a state of absolute mistrust and the civilian authorities were unable to guarantee the full safety of all citizens. For the reason -- for this reason they had approved requests for relocation of some parts of BH inhabitants abroad, wherever people asked to go. During the meeting, it was agreed to put Prijedor municipality in charge of the clearing up of the terrain because it was known that the perpetrators of the crime were from its territory. It was also concluded that the bodies should be identified at the scene and that the cause of death should be determined for each person. Furthermore, representatives of the prosecutor's office and the police were to investigate the event. The work of clearing up started on 4th of September, but were suspended when the crane used for lifting up posthumous remains broke down. Mr. Glamocic is not aware that anyone, either before, during, or after the meeting in Banja Luka, influenced the municipal authorities of Knezevo to hide anything in connection with the incident. On the contrary, everyone condemned the crime and demanded the punishment of the perpetrators. When the meeting finished, all the participants visited Knezevo and Koricanske Stijene. On that occasion, the commander of the 22nd Infantry Brigade of the VRS refused to receive the delegation from Banja Luka since the VRS did not accept or recognise Subotic as a minister of the defence. As a result, the relationship between the local civilian authorities and the command of the 22nd Infantry Brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps was rather poor. And that is short summary, and at that moment I do not have additional questions for Mr. Glamocic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Glamocic, as you have noted your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written witness statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. File, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocic, you first learned about the Koricanske Stijene massacre from Radovan Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: He called you at 4.00 in the morning on the 23rd of August; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So this phone call took place approximately two days after the massacre which had happened on the 21st of August; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You immediately went to see the president of the Knezevo Municipal Assembly, Milan Komljenovic; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you told him that Radovan Karadzic had just called you about the incident at Koricanske Stijene; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Komljenovic testified here in this case and he gave a statement or he said the following, and that's P3768 at page 3: "Three or four months ago Vlado Glamocic admitted to me the following story which I heard for the first time. On the night of the massacre, Glamocic received an enraged telephone call from Radovan Karadzic demanding answers about the massacre and who was responsible for it ..." Now, Mr. Komljenovic's comment was made in December of 2009, so his evidence is that you related this story about the Karadzic phone call to him sometime in mid-2009. So my question to you is: Is it possible that your recollection regarding when you first told Mr. Komljenovic about the call from Karadzic is faulty and that you actually told him in 2009, not when you first saw him after the massacre around the 23rd of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: No. It was for that reason that I visited Milan Komljenovic who resided in a village between 12 and 15 kilometres halfway from Banja Luka to Knezevo. On that same morning I told him that the president had called me and asked me about the incident at Koricanske Stijene. At this point he told me that on the previous day he was in the Prijedor municipality and the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly and that he discussed the incident at Koricanske Stijene with some people. This is definitely how it happened and the reason why I went to see Mr. Komljenovic was that I had received that call from Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You gave a sworn statement to the BiH prosecutor in 2008 in connection with the investigation and prosecution of perpetrators of the massacre; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And did you tell the whole truth in that statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter number 22096, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocic, does this look familiar to you as a copy of that sworn statement that you gave?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at English page 4 and B/C/S page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We're going to look at the middle of the first paragraph in both the English and the B/C/S. Here you'll see that you say: "I think it was around 22/23 of August when I came back to Knezevo and when I learnt from Milan Komljenovic that on the location of Koricanske Stijene the Prijedor police, who escorted this convoy, singled out a certain number of men from the convoy and killed them on that spot ..." So in 2008 in your sworn statement to the BiH prosecutor, you didn't mention anything about receiving an angry phone call from the president in the middle of the night, but rather that you learned of the massacre from Mr. Komljenovic himself; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes. But nobody had asked me whether Mr. Karadzic had called. I learnt about the incident at Koricanske Stijene from Milan Komljenovic. I don't know if Mr. Karadzic knew about everything that had happened at Koricanske Stijene, but he was probably familiar with the events. After my visit to the home of Milan Komljenovic, I heard from him what had happened and who had done it and what he had done on the previous day to attend the scene and to have these people buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit that page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6672, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 2 at page 55, the witness said: I learnt about the course of events at Koricanske Stijene from Milan Komljenovic, not about the incident, but about the course of the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm having said so, Mr. Glamocic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. As of 23 August 1992, when you spoke to Mr. Komljenovic, you had learned that the perpetrators of the Koricanske Stijene massacre were members of the Prijedor police; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention to a meeting. I didn't see it mentioned in your statement, but before you attended the large meeting on the 30th of August, 1992, that was chaired by Bogdan Subotic, you attended an earlier meeting around the 24th of August in Stojan Zupljanin's office in the Banja Luka CSB; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: No. Milan Komljenovic attended the meeting, that particular one. I attended only one meeting which was chaired by Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Both Mr. Komljenovic and Nenad Krejic discussed this first meeting in the evidence that they've given here, and both of them say that you were there as well. That is, for the record, Komljenovic's amalgamated statement which is P3768, pages 2 to 3, paragraph 4; and transcript 20914 to 15 in his testimony. And for Nenad Krejic it's P3760, e-court pages 21 to 23, which is his testimony from the Stanisic and Zupljanin case. Now, I just want to focus on a couple of details from Nenad Krejic's testimony, just to see if that might jog your memory about this meeting. He specifically mentions you being there, and then he says that you and Komljenovic nearly had a physical fight with Simo Drljaca over the issue of who would be responsible for removing the bodies, that's at page 23 of his testimony. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: We did experience conflicts in communication with the municipality of Prijedor, in particular with Simo and Stakic, but I recall our conflicts and misunderstandings happening at this meeting chaired by Mr. Subotic. And this had a bearing on our visit to Koricanske Stijene and all the other things that Simo Drljaca did together with his people at Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: I don't remember this meeting. As for the other meeting that was chaired by Mr. Subotic, I kept notes for the part of the -- for a part of the meeting and conclusions were formulated by Mr. Komljenovic and we used the same notebook for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that meeting in just a minute. Nenad Krejic also said at the same page that Drljaca and Stakic admitted that the Prijedor police had committed this crime and that Drljaca was bragging about it. Do you recall ever hearing something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe that he was bragging about it. It was not a thing to brag about. What Simo insisted on and opposed our suggestion and demand that they clear out the terrain and that they remove the bodies, so they opposed this idea because the Knezevo municipality didn't have either the human or material resources to do the job. Simo Drljaca would at times attack our people from the civilian protection, Mr. Barisic, who was the chief, with some very strong language.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 32 of your statement you say: "During my encounters with Drljaca, I gained an impression that he was furious because this crime had happened ..." But isn't it possible that Drljaca was angry instead that your municipality was not willing to clean up the site of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think Drljaca was angry with the perpetrators of the crime. He was, second of all, probably angry because we weren't able to do the job and this was our unambiguous position as was of the command of the 22nd Brigade as well as the population of the Knezevo municipality in general. I don't believe that Simo was angry at us, but rather I think he was angry with the perpetrators of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to the 30th of August, 1992, meeting that was chaired by Subotic. One of the conclusions of that meeting you say in your statement at paragraph 28 is: "It was agreed to put Prijedor municipality in charge of the clearing up of the terrain because it was known that the perpetrators of the crime were from its territory." Now, that is understating what was known at the time, right, because everybody in that meeting knew that it wasn't just that the perpetrators were from the territory of Prijedor, they were members of the Prijedor police; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, another conclusion of this meeting is at paragraph 28 of your statement. You say: "It was also concluded that the bodies should be identified at the scene. Pathologists engaged to determine the exact cause of death for each person ..." And then at paragraph 33 of your statement you say: "As far as I know, a crane was set up on the road and it was to be used to lift up posthumous remains ..." Now, I'm going to show you a video that will last for just over 3 minutes and I'm going to ask you a few questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is going to be 65 ter 40573D which is time-code 55.30 to 58.48.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, this video depicts Koricanske Stijene; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And in this video you can see the recovery of three bodies using the crane that you described in your statement. Now, you would agree that this does not look like people who are under instructions to preserve bodies for a pathologist to examine them for the cause of death or for them to be identified; right? This looks more like disposing of garbage, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6673, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, may I just make a comment? It's an ugly sight. Your question that this looks more like disposing of garbage, you have to understand that the terrain is extremely difficult. There was just this narrow path from the access road from where this crane was operating, and also the depth from which the bodies were being taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another topic. In your statement at paragraph 30 you describe how the commander of the 22nd Infantry Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Bosko Peulic, who was the local VRS commander, refused to receive the delegation from Banja Luka in the brigade because the VRS did not accept or recognise Bogdan Subotic as minister of defence. And then in paragraph 31 you describe how: "The relationship between the local civilian authorities and the command of the 22nd pbr of the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS was rather poor as a result of the poor relationship between the brigade commander and the civilian authorities ..." You go on to describe how the brigade commander Peulic was difficult to work with. And then you say: "In addition to these disagreements, there were purely ideological matters which were, in my opinion, none of his business."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'd like to bring up 65 ter 26025, please. I'm just going to show you three small portions of testimony that Colonel Peulic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I would like you to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm going to show you three small portions of testimony that Colonel Peulic gave in one of the BiH court trials of perpetrators of the Koricanske Stijene massacre, and then I'm going to ask you a question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could have English page 14 and B/C/S page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We're going to focus on the middle of the English page and the top of the B/C/S page. Here you'll see a question from the Prosecutor to

utterances.speaker: MR. PEULIC
utterances.text: "Did you receive such an order," he's referring to the minister of defence, Subotic, "for clearing up from the Minister, as a military insubordination?" And Peulic answers: "No, no, I think that I promptly let him know, I didn't on principle honour such orders ever, especially not when such a difficult matter was at issue. I knew that any order which represents a crime pursuant to the Rules of Service in the JNA, a commander and indeed any serviceman can refuse such an order, namely, an order which represents a crime. Participation in such a serious matter would mean my co-perpetration in a crime and so on and consequently it fell on stoney ground with me ..." The next passage I want to show you is on the next page in both versions. In the middle of both pages. Here he's describing -- the prosecutor's asking about a meeting that Peulic attended that took place in the Alumina factory approximately three days after the massacre. He says it was attended by you as well as Komljenovic, Stakic, and Drljaca. And the witness says: "Well, the meeting set off in a somewhat non-parliamentary manner, as I'd call it. It began with an exchange of information about what should be done and so on. Suddenly this other stouter man Simo Drljaca banged his fist on the table and said: 'We did our part and what did you do?'" And if we can continue on to the top of the B/C/S page 22. When he's asked what he understood this to mean, he said: Well, that he meant: Well, we killed them, you clear it up. First of all, do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And do you remember it roughly as Mr. Peulic described it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we can just go to English page 24, B/C/S page 35. We're going to focus on the lower half of both pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
