utterances.text: This part of the testimony refers to a telegram that Peulic had sent on the night of the massacre, 21st August, 1992, to the 1 KK command intelligence security department. That telegram is in our case in evidence as Exhibit D2040. You'll see the judge asks: "Do you agree that you wrote what it says in there that night that genocide had been done?" The witness says: "That's it." The judge says: "All right." And then the counsel asks: "Mr. Peulic, what I would like to know is, at that -- at that at that moment, I don't know what your function in the army was, did you know what the word 'genocide' meant?" And if we go to the top of page 36 in the B/C/S. Peulic answers: "I did." Then he's asked: "You knew what it meant?" He answers: "Yes." And then he's asked: "And you found that it was genocide?" And he answers: "I still do." So my question to you is: Do you think that it's possible that Colonel Peulic may have proven difficult to work with and may have had what you call ideological differences with civilian authorities because he thought this was a case of genocide and he felt he was being pressured to participate in some form of cover-up and he wanted to have nothing to do with it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: No, this statement of mine did not pertain only to the problem of Koricanske Stijene when I spoke about this difficult co-operation with the army, it had to do with the number of persons involved. At the time the economy was functioning and the army was asking for a lot of resources, material, technical. Mr. Peulic attended a meeting with us in Banja Luka and the conclusion of that meeting was that we should all go to the location of Koricanske Stijene. All of the attendees from the meeting went to Koricanske Stijene. It was agreed that in the meantime we should meet at the command of the 22nd Brigade that was commanded by Peulic. Peulic didn't want to wait for us at the command of the 22nd Brigade. We organised that meeting at a different location, at the command of the light brigade. It is correct that Peulic didn't want to hear of any participation of the military in the sanitisation of the terrain, or rather, recovering the corpses, things that the army would deal with in that situation. He knew who the perpetrators were. So he did not dream of using the assets that the army had available. I want to say that the area of Koricanske Stijene did not belong to the municipality of Knezevo. The area of Koricanske Stijene belonged to the municipality of Travnik, so this was a war zone of this 22nd Brigade. And we, as the civilian authorities, when we would go to the command of that brigade, we would have to be announced to the command of that brigade. So it was a war zone. This territory did not belong to the municipality of Knezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. The last topic I'd like to explore with you relates to paragraph 33 of your statement. You say: "At one point when the crane was working an ambulance transporting wounded people came up but could not get past the crane. While the crane was being removed from the road, it broke down, and despite all the efforts it could not be repaired. As a result, work on the removal of posthumous remains was suspended ..." And then that's the conclusion of your witness statement. But it seems like an odd point to end the story in your statement because there were frequent complaints of the smell and possible water contamination - you acknowledge that in paragraph 21 of your statement - animals and birds were depositing human remains on the roof-tops of nearby residents of Koricani village - that's in P3760 at page 39 - the situation in this area was intolerable and it was imperative to make this problem go away. So what happened to the bodies afterwards? They weren't just left out there to continue decomposing; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the civilian protection department of the municipality of Knezevo buried four mortal remains that were identified and that was done in accordance with the conclusions of the CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Right. But there were 150 to 200 bodies out there, so what happened to those?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: I don't have the exact information on this. All I know is what was written in the press in "Nezavisne Novine" from Banja Luka. Because with regard to all of these activities it was the investigating judge who was in charge as well as the prosecutor and the crime inspector from the CSB, and with Simo Drljaca they were in charge of these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: As chairman of the executive committee of the Municipal Assembly, the IO SO, by law you were the commander of the civilian protection, or CZ, in the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you were able to give orders and instructions to the chief of the civilian protection of Knezevo municipality?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So this is a horrific mass crime as well as a potential public health crisis in the municipality where you're the chairman of the Executive Committee. The police from another municipality have caused it and now they are tasked with cleaning it up. My question is: Under those circumstances, don't you just want to make sure they're doing their job properly? All you had to do was to tell Barisic, the head of the CZ, to go over there and see what they're doing and report back to you; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Barisic was at Koricanske Stijene with the civilian protection unit several times. He did not have enough manpower. He did not have enough material resources and he was not able to do anything more meaningful than what he had done. He always had a problem with Simo Drljaca. As a matter of fact, he was even chasing them away from the scene. The civilian protection of Knezevo was supposed to provide accommodation for the people from Prijedor. We did that at the school in Limeni [phoen] and that is our only obligation in addition to the obligation from the Banja Luka meeting, namely that the civilian protection from the municipality of Knezevo should dig graves and bury all the persons who are identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: According to Komljenovic, some of your civilian protection people were always present on the site during the clean-up operation, that's in P3768 at e-court page 11. He says that the Prijedor team had brought some equipment from the Prijedor mines, tried to do the job, the crane broke down, they couldn't do the job. Then he says: Those are the things that we heard indirectly about what had been going on up there because even some of our own people from civilian protection were always present there, so to some extent we were able to see what was going on. So regardless of whether civilian protection had difficulty working with Drljaca or had limited responsibilities there, you still had a source of information for what was going to happen to these bodies; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Barisic could convey only what he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 29 - this is my last question - you said: "I'm not aware that anyone, either before, during, or after the meeting in Banja Luka, influenced the municipal authorities of Knezevo to hide anything in connection with the incident. On the contrary, everyone was repulsed and condemned this crime and demanded that those responsible be punished." But if that was really true, if everybody was repulsed by this, if everybody condemned the crime and wanted to assure accountability, if nobody wanted to hide anything, don't you think that at a bare minimum there should have been public information about where the bodies had been buried for the families of all these victims? We found out about the location of the burial site in 2009 from a perpetrator in a confession. We shouldn't have had to wait that long; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Well, the media did inform the public. That was in two articles in "Nezavisne Novine." There was no wish from any side, least of all from the executive authorities of the municipality of Knezevo, to hide the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But we're talking about the burial site -- the mass burial site with more than a hundred bodies, that information never came out until 2009; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Then my last question will be about 65 ter number 26023. This is an article describing the exhumation of a mass grave at Koricanske Stijene from 21st July 2009. It says in the middle of the page: "Damir Ivankovic was originally among the indictees charged with this crime. He admitted guilt and concluded an agreement with the Prosecution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After accepting the agreement, the Trial Chamber sentenced him to 14 years in prison. "Ivankovic testified against the seven indictees charged under the same indictment. After this, a new indictment against two former members of the Emergency Squad was filed. "The locations of mass graves were identified on the basis of Ivankovic's statement." Is this the first time that you're hearing about this, Mr. Glamocic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: I first heard of the information about the location of the grave from the article in "Nezavisne Novine." I don't remember the exact year.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, shall we continue after the break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I could have finished within this session if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much would you need, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Glamocic, since the document is here now, where were you, where did you live, and what were you doing, what was your job, in 2009 when this exhumation took place?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: In 2009 I worked in the public company for roads in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did you live and where is this company located?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: I lived and worked in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 61/62 of the transcript what was put to you was the testimony of Mr. Peulic and what Drljaca said. Was it your understanding that in this way Drljaca stated that he had ordered the killing?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: No, no. Simo Drljaca was embittered because of what had happened. I cannot say whether he approved or not, but he was embittered like all of us. And I never had the impression that it was Simo who ordered or organised that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 65 you were asked about what your civilian protection did. Did your civilian protection have authority over parts of the municipality of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: I've already said that Koricanske Stijene and Koricani did not belong to the municipality of Knezevo. It was just the war zone of the 22nd Brigade. So this did not belong to the municipality of Knezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about now?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: Now this area does belong to Knezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When were they attached to Knezevo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GLAMOCIC
utterances.text: After the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Glamocic. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go, but we'll rise all together. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't have any further witnesses for today. The next witness is scheduled to testify first thing tomorrow morning, so if -- I think we have to adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even the Witness 584?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness 584 is from the Croatian government and they've not had any contact with us, so all we can hope for is that he will appear at 9.00 tomorrow as requested; if not, we will be filing a motion that he be subpoenaed but we have no information from him at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just so there's no misunderstanding on the Court's part, the next witness who Mr. Robinson was referring to is Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's unfortunate he's not here now, but that's the situation, I gather, we find ourselves in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, unless there's any other matters to raise, the hearing is adjourned for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of February, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.41 p.m.,
